principleDraft.title: Gate Evidence at Entry: Unverifiable Inputs Must Not Propagate as Verified Conclusions

At merge points where multiple submission channels with heterogeneous provenance guarantees converge, the weakest channel must never silently define the confidence of the merged conclusion; provenance must be captured and persisted at input time, not reconstructed after the fact.
principleDraft.rationale: The root cause was that an input lacking observable provenance was accepted as a normal-confidence input, its weakness was buried in internal notes, and the derived output propagated downstream as if verified. Gating at the entry point, persisting provenance at capture time, and attaching enforceable evidence-strength labels (with refusal or a hard confidence ceiling when evidence falls below threshold) converts a silent epistemic degradation into an explicit, blocked, or clearly-marked condition that every downstream consumer can see and act on.
applicability: Data, claims, or reports entering a diagnosis, analysis, automated-decisioning, or reporting pipeline whose outputs downstream consumers treat as verified

Runtime contexts where trace evidence or authenticated sessions may be unavailable at the moment of submission
Merge points where inputs from different channels combine into a shared conclusion or confidence score
antiPatterns: Accepting an unverifiable input at normal confidence and noting its weakness only in internal notes while the output propagates downstream as if verified
Letting the weakest channel's provenance silently define the confidence of merged conclusions

Attempting to reconstruct provenance after processing instead of capturing and persisting it at input entry

intentContract.targetBehavior: Before ingesting any input, the agent verifies or captures and persists its provenance at entry; when provenance is unverifiable, the agent either refuses/quarantines the input or processes it under a machine-checkable reduced-evidence label with a hard confidence ceiling, and records the gating decision and label in persisted state so downstream consumers can observe it.
intentContract.forbiddenBehavior: Accepting an unverifiable input as a normal-confidence input, burying its weakness in internal notes, and letting the derived output propagate downstream as a verified conclusion — including silently allowing the weakest submission channel to set the confidence of merged results.

risks: Partially overlaps with core axioms T-03 (use observable evidence before claiming results), T-05 (translate hard constraints into explicit guardrails), and T-10 (persist important state); rule generation must define precedence to avoid redundant or conflicting enforcement.
Fail-closed gating can block legitimate owner-reported inputs when instrumentation or authenticated sessions are unavailable, reducing availability and frustrating owners.
Evidence-strength labels can create a false sense of safety if downstream consumers ignore them; labeling without enforcement does not prevent misuse.
Aggressive refusal thresholds may push users to bypass official channels entirely, degrading overall observability rather than improving it.

Over-broad application could gate informal collaborative or exploratory inputs where provenance is naturally weak, adding friction without epistemic benefit; applicability should stay scoped to pipelines whose outputs are treated as verified.

principleDraft.title: Bind Inference Depth to Verified Evidence Grade at Pipeline Entry
principleDraft.statement: At every ingestion boundary of a pipeline that produces consequential conclusions or actions, the system must assign each input an explicit evidence grade derived from verifiable provenance (e.g., an authenticated session with an observable behavioral trace), durably persist that grade and its provenance with the payload, and enforce a gate that permits the transition into full-depth processing only when the required grade is present. When evidence is absent or unverifiable, the gate must halt and request re-submission with verifiable evidence, or route the input to an explicitly downgraded mode that emits hypothesis-level output with labeled provenance and reduced confidence. The system must never continue at full depth on unverifiable input, and must never rely on downstream actor discretion to compensate for missing evidence.
principleDraft.rationale: The diagnosed root cause was structural, not a judgment lapse: the CLI submission path allowed a pain report whose trace was 'unavailable_with_reason' and that carried no authenticated session provenance to enter the diagnosis pipeline, where full-depth causal inference proceeded on owner report alone. Binding inference depth and confidence to a persisted evidence grade via an enforceable entry gate makes it structurally impossible for conclusions to outrun their evidence, regardless of downstream actor judgment or context loss.

parsed.thesis: Trustworthy conclusions are secured at the point of evidence capture, not recovered at the point of use. When downstream reasoning depends on upstream evidence, systems should bind verifiable evidence to claims at intake, translate evidence requirements into entry-point guardrails, honestly grade confidence when evidence is absent, persist the state needed for later verification, and recycle recurring evidence-related friction into design-level fixes.

principleCandidate.title: Gate evidence at intake; grade confidence honestly when evidence is absent
principleCandidate.rationale: The recurring root cause across all Dreamer candidates is that evidence requirements were discovered missing downstream during diagnosis rather than guaranteed upstream at submission. Enforcing evidence binding at the entry point (session/context gating, explicit validation rules, forbidden transitions) prevents unverifiable claims from entering high-confidence workflows, and when evidence genuinely cannot be captured, explicitly labeling conclusions as low-confidence with a labeled evidence tier keeps downstream consumers from mistaking inference for verified fact. Entry gating is also the minimal intervention: it stops the defect at the source rather than spending diagnostic resources discovering it late.
principleCandidate.scope: Applies wherever a downstream reasoning, diagnostic, or verification step depends on evidence captured at an earlier intake point—report submission, data ingestion, state capture, handoffs between subsystems—especially when multiple ingestion paths exist with differing evidentiary capability (e.g., authenticated vs. unauthenticated, instrumented vs. bare). Also applies when intermediate conclusions and traces must persist for later auditability.

risks: Substantial overlap with core axioms T-03 (use observable evidence before inferring causes) and T-05 (translate hard constraints into explicit guardrails before execution); this candidate primarily re-locates their application to the intake point and may be redundant with existing axioms.
Strict entry gating can reject legitimate reports during transient evidence-capture failures, trading availability and accessibility for verifiability.
Confidence-grade or evidence-tier labels may be ignored or stripped by downstream consumers, creating false assurance despite honest labeling at the source.
Persisting traces, submission context, and intermediate conclusions for auditability increases storage, privacy, and retention-management burden.
Gating design may entrench a single privileged ingestion path, discouraging alternative low-evidence paths instead of formally defining their degraded evidence tier.

principleDraft.title: Bind evidence to claims at intake; grade confidence when evidence is absent
principleDraft.statement: Whenever a downstream reasoning, diagnostic, or verification step depends on evidence captured at an earlier intake point (submission, ingestion, state capture, subsystem handoff), the intake step must bind verifiable evidence (identity, context, traces) to the incoming claim as an entry-point guardrail, and when evidence genuinely cannot be captured, must attach an explicit evidence-tier/confidence label marking the claim as evidence-absent before it proceeds; unlabeled evidence-free claims must never enter high-confidence workflows.
principleDraft.rationale: The recurring root cause across the Dreamer candidates is that evidence requirements were discovered missing downstream during diagnosis rather than guaranteed upstream at submission. Gating at intake stops the defect at the source, which is also the minimal intervention compared to spending diagnostic resources discovering missing evidence late. When evidence cannot be captured, honest confidence grading at intake prevents downstream consumers from mistaking inference for verified fact.
applicability: Report or claim submission and data ingestion where downstream diagnosis or verification depends on captured evidence
Handoffs between subsystems where upstream-captured state or context is consumed downstream
Systems with multiple ingestion paths of differing evidentiary capability (authenticated vs. unauthenticated, instrumented vs. bare)
Pipelines where intermediate conclusions, submission context, or traces must persist for later auditability
Any workflow where confidence labels propagate into downstream decision-making
antiPatterns: Accepting claims into high-confidence workflows without bound evidence or an explicit evidence tier attached at intake
Discovering evidence requirements only post-hoc during downstream diagnosis instead of enforcing them at the entry point
Silently promoting inference to verified-fact status by stripping or ignoring confidence/evidence-tier labels
Designing gated intake as a single privileged path with no formally defined degraded tier for low-evidence submissions
Discarding submission context and traces that later verification or audit would require

intentContract.ownerIntent: The Owner wants claims admitted into downstream reasoning only when verifiable evidence is bound to them at the intake point, or when that is impossible, only with an explicit evidence-absent/low-confidence label so inference is never mistaken for verified fact.
intentContract.targetBehavior: At every intake point (submission, ingestion, handoff), a compliant agent checks that required evidence is attached before passing the claim downstream; if evidence is missing, it captures it, rejects the transition, or attaches an explicit evidence-tier/confidence label, and persists the evidence state needed for later verification.
intentContract.forbiddenBehavior: Allowing evidence-free claims to enter downstream diagnostic or verification workflows unlabeled, such that missing evidence is only discovered during downstream diagnosis and inference is consumed as verified fact.
intentContract.evidenceSource: The philosopher diagnosis (pi-art-philosopher-pri815-G-manual_1788265732489_9ne-r3-run1) that the recurring root cause across Dreamer candidates was evidence requirements discovered missing downstream during diagnosis rather than guaranteed upstream at submission, across multi-path ingestion contexts with differing evidentiary capability.
intentContract.validationExpectation: An evaluator should verify that any generated rule enforces an intake-time check — evidence bound or an evidence-absent tier attached — before downstream use, that unlabeled evidence-free claims are rejected or downgraded, and that the rule does not rely on post-hoc downstream detection of missing evidence.

risks: Substantial overlap with core axioms T-03 (use observable evidence before inferring causes) and T-05 (translate hard constraints into explicit guardrails before execution): this principle mainly re-locates their application to the intake point; downstream stages must confirm it adds entry-point specificity rather than duplicating existing axiom coverage.
Strict intake gating may reject legitimate submissions during transient evidence-capture failures, trading availability and accessibility for verifiability.
Downstream consumers may ignore or strip confidence/evidence-tier labels, creating false assurance despite honest labeling at the source.
Persisting traces, submission context, and intermediate conclusions for auditability increases storage, privacy, and retention-management burden.
Gating design may entrench a single privileged ingestion path unless degraded evidence tiers are formally defined for alternative low-evidence paths.
Rule generation may over-generalize the evidence requirement to trivial, low-stakes claims, adding friction where full evidence binding is disproportionate.

principleDraft.title: Gate evidence at intake; block or explicitly downgrade conclusions lacking evidence
principleDraft.statement: Whenever a downstream reasoning, diagnostic, or verification step depends on evidence captured at an earlier intake point, the intake point must enforce an evidence-availability gate: either verifiable evidence (e.g., an authenticated session trace) is bound to the submission at intake, or the submission is barred from high-confidence processing paths and any conclusion drawn from it is explicitly labeled with a downgraded evidence tier (e.g., owner-inference-only).
principleDraft.rationale: The diagnosed root cause is a design gap: pain reports could be submitted from a non-authenticated path (CLI) without mandatory session binding or observable trace, so diagnosis proceeded on unverifiable owner-reported inference and the state needed to verify it was never captured (violating T-03 and T-10). Enforcing the evidence requirement as an entry-point gate with a forbidden transition stops unverifiable claims at the source — the minimal intervention — rather than discovering missing evidence downstream, and explicit downgraded evidence labels prevent downstream consumers from mistaking inference for verified fact when evidence genuinely cannot be captured.
applicability: Entry points feeding diagnosis or verification workflows: pain-report submission, data ingestion, state capture, subsystem handoffs
Systems with multiple ingestion paths of differing evidentiary capability (e.g., authenticated session vs. CLI/non-session submission)
Any conclusion handed to downstream consumers when observable evidence is genuinely unavailable and only inference remains
Workflows where traces, submission context, and intermediate conclusions must persist for later auditability
antiPatterns: Accepting submissions from any path into full-confidence diagnosis without an intake check for observable evidence
Proceeding with diagnosis or conclusions at normal confidence when the only evidence is owner-reported inference with no behavioral trace
Leaving evidence availability to be discovered downstream, after the intake point has already failed to capture or bind the needed state
Rejecting or downgrading silently: no explicit evidence-tier label on conclusions and no instruction to resubmit from an evidence-capable path
Relying on process convention instead of an enforced entry-point check or forbidden transition

intentContract.ownerIntent: Pain reports and other diagnostic inputs must arrive with verifiable session-trace evidence bound at submission, so no diagnosis is presented as verified when it actually rests on unverifiable owner report.
intentContract.targetBehavior: Before a submission enters a diagnostic or reasoning workflow, the agent checks evidence availability at the intake point: with an authenticated trace bound, it proceeds; without one, it either blocks the submission and directs the reporter to resubmit from an authenticated session, or processes it under an explicit low-confidence, owner-inference-only evidence label attached to the conclusion.
intentContract.forbiddenBehavior: Letting unevidenced submissions from non-authenticated paths flow into full-confidence diagnosis, so conclusions are asserted without observable evidence and the evidence gap is only discovered downstream during diagnosis.
intentContract.evidenceSource: Diagnosis manual_1788265732489_9nexm9e6: a CLI-submitted pain report with no authenticated host-session provenance, trace marked unavailable_with_reason, nextAction advising resubmission from an OpenClaw session or owner-reason-only diagnosis, and a strong intentTension between evidence requirements and the CLI path (T-03/T-10 violations).
intentContract.validationExpectation: An evaluator should see the rule act before diagnosis begins: a visible intake check for trace/session binding, followed by either a rejection with resubmission guidance or an explicit downgraded evidence tier carried on the conclusion. A rule that only requests evidence after diagnosis has started, or that lets unbound submissions through at full confidence, is unfaithful to this intent.

risks: Substantial overlap with core axioms T-03 (observable evidence before inference), T-05 (hard constraints as explicit guardrails) and T-10 (persist critical state); this principle mainly re-locates them to the intake point and may be redundant with existing axioms.
Strict entry gating can reject legitimate submissions during transient evidence-capture failures, trading availability and accessibility for verifiability.
Downgraded evidence-tier labels may be ignored or stripped by downstream consumers, creating false assurance despite honest labeling at the source.

The diagnosis flagged unresolved intentTension (suggestedOwnerAction: revise_intent): the owner has not yet decided whether to block the CLI path or formally define its degraded evidence tier, so the principle risks entrenching one choice prematurely.
Binding traces and persisting submission context for auditability increases storage, privacy, and retention-management burden.
Gating may entrench a single privileged ingestion path and discourage formally defining low-evidence alternative paths.
